questions.question: How many Cl$^-$ ions are there around Na$^+$ ion in NaCl crystal?
questions.answer:
**(C)** 6

NaCl has the rock-salt (f.c.c.) structure in which each Na$^+$ sits in an octahedral hole surrounded by six Cl$^-$ ions — the coordination number of both ions is 6. The ions lie along the three cube axes, $3+3=6$ Cl$^-$ around each Na$^+$, and the structure can be regarded as two interpenetrating f.c.c. lattices.

questions.question: The material used in the solar cells contains:
questions.answer:
**(B)** Si

Solar cells are made of semiconducting **silicon** — usually doped p-type and n-type to form a p-n junction. Photons with energy greater than the band gap ($\approx1.1$ eV) create electron-hole pairs, the junction field separates them and a photovoltage appears. Caesium, tin and titanium do not have a suitable band gap for this.

questions.question: A first-order reaction has a half-life period 34.65 seconds. Its rate constant is:
questions.answer:
**(A)** $2\times10^{-2}\ \text{s}^{-1}$

For a first-order reaction the half-life is independent of concentration:

$$k=\frac{0.693}{t_{1/2}}=\frac{0.693}{34.65}=2\times10^{-2}\ \text{s}^{-1}$$

(The printed key also gives (i).) Note that $t_{1/2}$ here is close to $100\ln2$ seconds, which is why the answer comes out as a neat power of ten.

questions.question: If a graph is plotted between $\ln k$ and $1/T$ for the first-order reaction, the slope of the straight line so obtained is given by:
questions.answer:
**(A)** $-\dfrac{E_a}{R}$

Taking logarithms of the Arrhenius equation $k=Ae^{-E_a/RT}$,

$$\ln k=\ln A-\frac{E_a}{R}\cdot\frac1T$$

so a plot of $\ln k$ against $1/T$ is a straight line of slope $-E_a/R$ and intercept $\ln A$. (If $\log_{10}k$ is plotted instead, the slope is $-E_a/2.303R$ — that is where option (B) comes from, but the question uses $\ln$.)

questions.question: Which element is kept in water?
questions.answer:
**(A)** P

White phosphorus is highly reactive towards oxygen and ignites spontaneously in air at about 30 °C, so it is stored **under water**, which cuts off the air and protects it. Sodium is stored under kerosene (it reacts violently with water), and sulphur and silicon need no such protection.

questions.question: Aldol is a condensation product of:
questions.answer:
**(B)** Two molecules of propanone

Aldol condensation needs a carbonyl compound with at least one $\alpha$-hydrogen. Dilute alkali removes an $\alpha$-H from one molecule, the resulting carbanion attacks the carbonyl carbon of a second molecule, and a $\beta$-hydroxy carbonyl (an "aldol") is formed; with propanone the product is diacetone alcohol, CH$_3$COCH$_2$C(OH)(CH$_3$)$_2$:

$$\underset{	ext{diacetone alcohol}}{\ce{(CH3)2C(OH)CH2COCH3}}$$

Ethanol contains no carbonyl group at all and cannot undergo aldol condensation.

*Note on the printed key:* the paper marks (a) (ethanol), which is chemically impossible; the intended answer is the ketone, option (B).

questions.question: The amino acids are the end product of the digestion of:
questions.answer:
**(C)** Protein

Proteins are polymers of $\alpha$-amino acids joined by peptide bonds. Digestion hydrolyses these bonds — pepsin in the stomach, then trypsin and peptidases in the small intestine — until free amino acids are released, which are absorbed and used to build new proteins. Fats and lipids are broken down to fatty acids and glycerol, not to amino acids.

questions.question: When primary amine reacts with chloroform in ethanolic KOH, then the product is:
questions.answer:
**(A)** Isocyanide

This is the **carbylamine (Hoffmann isocyanide) test**, given only by primary amines, including aniline:

$$\ce{RNH2 + CHCl3 + 3KOH_{(alc)} -> R-NC + 3KCl + 3H2O}$$

The product is an alkyl (or aryl) isocyanide, $\ce{R-NC}$, which has a foul, characteristic smell — the basis of the test. Secondary and tertiary amines do not give it.

questions.question: What is Schottky defect?
questions.answer:
**Schottky defect** is a point defect in ionic crystals in which **equal numbers of cations and anions are missing** from their normal lattice sites, leaving equal numbers of cation and anion vacancies.

Because the missing ions carry opposite charges, the crystal stays electrically neutral, but its density decreases and its lattice energy falls. The vacancies are also the route for ionic conduction. It occurs in highly ionic salts with similar cation and anion sizes and high coordination numbers — NaCl, KCl, KBr and CsCl.

questions.question: Explain the terms: (a) specific conductivity (b) equivalent conductivity.
questions.answer:
**(a) Specific conductivity ($\kappa$).** The conductance of a column of the solution 1 cm long and of 1 cm$^2$ cross-section, i.e. of one cubic centimetre of solution. Since $R=\rho\,l/a$,

$$\kappa=\frac{1}{\rho}=\frac{1}{R}\cdot\frac{l}{a}=G\times\text{cell constant}$$

Its unit is $\Omega^{-1}\text{cm}^{-1}$ (S cm$^{-1}$). It decreases with dilution because the number of ions per unit volume falls.

**(b) Equivalent conductivity ($\Lambda$).** The conductance of a solution containing one gram equivalent of the electrolyte placed between electrodes 1 cm apart:

$$\Lambda=\frac{\kappa\times1000}{C}$$

with $C$ in equivalents per litre, giving units $\Omega^{-1}\text{cm}^{2}\text{eq}^{-1}$. Unlike $\kappa$, $\Lambda$ *increases* with dilution and approaches a limiting value $\Lambda_\infty$ at infinite dilution (Kohlrausch's law).

questions.question: Write any two features that distinguish physisorption from chemisorption.
questions.answer:
| Physisorption | Chemisorption |
|---|---|
| Caused by weak van der Waals forces | Caused by strong forces, of the order of a chemical bond |
| Low heat of adsorption, about 20–40 kJ/mol | High heat of adsorption, about 80–240 kJ/mol |
| Occurs at low temperature and is reversible; multilayer possible | Needs high temperature, is largely irreversible; monolayer only |
| No activation energy; not specific | Has an activation energy and is highly specific |

*Any two of the above contrasted pairs.* A simple illustration: hydrogen on charcoal is physisorbed by weak van der Waals forces, while hydrogen on nickel is chemisorbed as Ni–H bonds.

questions.question: State Hardy-Schulze rule.
questions.answer:
**Hardy–Schulze rule:** the coagulating (precipitating) power of an ion depends on the magnitude of its charge — *the greater the valency of the flocculating ion added, the greater is its power to cause precipitation of a colloidal sol.*

For a negatively charged sol (e.g. As$_2$S$_3$) the effective ions are cations, and their coagulating power is in the order $\ce{Al^{3+}>Ba^{2+}>Na^{+}}$; for a positively charged sol (e.g. Fe(OH)$_3$) the order is $\ce{[Fe(CN)6]^{4-}>PO4^{3-}>SO4^{2-}>Cl^{-}}$. Roughly, the coagulating power increases as the sixth power of the valency (Schulze–Hardy proportionality).

questions.question: Write the laboratory method of the preparation of phosphine with equation (only principle).
questions.answer:
**Principle:** white phosphorus is boiled with concentrated NaOH solution in an **inert atmosphere** (of $\ce{CO2}$ or coal gas) — air must be excluded because phosphine is spontaneously flammable in air:

$$\ce{P4 + 3NaOH + 3H2O -> 2NaH2PO2 + PH3}$$ Sodium hypophosphite and phosphine are formed.

The impure gas also contains $\ce{P2H4}$ (diphosphine) vapour, which ignites spontaneously in air and makes the gas burn with smoky rings; passing it through a freezing mixture removes $\ce{P2H4}$, and the pure $\ce{PH3}$ obtained does not ignite in air below 150 °C.

questions.question: Write the balanced equation for the following: (a) NaCl is heated with sulphuric acid in the presence of MnO$_2$. (b) Iodine is treated with concentrated HNO$_3$.
questions.answer:
**(a) NaCl + conc. H$_2$SO$_4$ with MnO$_2$** — this is the laboratory preparation of chlorine:

$$\ce{2NaCl + MnO2 + 3H2SO4 -> 2NaHSO4 + MnSO4 + Cl2 + 2H2O}$$

The MnO$_2$ oxidises the HCl formed *in situ* to Cl$_2$; the NaHSO$_4$ stays in solution.

**(b) Iodine with concentrated nitric acid** — iodine is oxidised to iodic acid:

$$\ce{I2 + 10HNO3 -> 2HIO3 + 10NO2 + 4H2O}$$

The nitric acid is reduced to brown NO$_2$ fumes, which is why this reaction is used as a test for iodine.

questions.question: Identify A and B in the following sequence: $\ce{CH3-CH=CH2 ->[HBr] A ->[alc.KOH] B}$
questions.answer:
**A = 2-bromopropane**, CH$_3$-CHBr-CH$_3$
**B = propene**, CH$_3$-CH=CH$_2$

Step 1 follows **Markovnikov's rule**: the H of HBr adds to the carbon carrying more hydrogens, so Br goes to the middle (more substituted) carbon — the secondary carbocation is more stable:

$$\ce{CH3-CH=CH2 + HBr -> CH3-CHBr-CH3}$$

Step 2 is **dehydrohalogenation** by alcoholic KOH (an elimination), which removes HBr and regenerates the alkene:

$$\ce{CH3-CHBr-CH3 ->[alc. KOH] CH3-CH=CH2 + KBr + H2O}$$

(Note that if peroxide were present in step 1 the addition would be anti-Markovnikov, giving 1-bromopropane.)

questions.question: Identify A and B: Chlorobenzene $\xrightarrow[623\ \text{K, pressure}]{\text{NaOH}}$ A $\xrightarrow{H^{+},H_2O}$ B
questions.answer:
**A = sodium phenoxide**, $\ce{C6H5ONa}$
**B = phenol**, $\ce{C6H5OH}$

This is the **Dow process**. Aryl halides are normally inert to nucleophilic substitution because of partial double-bond character of the C–Cl bond, so drastic conditions are needed — chlorobenzene with aqueous NaOH at 623 K and 300 atm gives sodium phenoxide by a benzyne/elimination–addition mechanism:

$$\ce{C6H5Cl + 2NaOH ->[623 K] C6H5ONa + NaCl + H2O}$$

Acidification of the phenoxide liberates the weakly acidic phenol:

$$\ce{C6H5ONa + HCl -> C6H5OH + NaCl}$$

questions.question: Give an example of Kolbe reaction.
questions.answer:
**Kolbe's electrolytic reaction** — the aqueous solution of a sodium or potassium carboxylate is electrolysed and the carboxylate groups are lost as $\ce{CO2}$ at the anode, the alkyl groups joining to give an alkane:

$$\ce{2CH3COONa + 2H2O ->[electrolysis] CH3-CH3 + 2CO2 + H2 + 2NaOH}$$

**Anode:** $\ce{2CH3COO^{-} -> CH3-CH3 + 2CO2 + 2e^{-}}$
**Cathode:** $\ce{2Na+ + 2e^- -> 2Na}$, and $\ce{2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2}$

This is a standard laboratory route to ethane (and, with a longer chain carboxylate, to other symmetrical alkanes).

questions.question: Give an example of Reimer-Tiemann reaction.
questions.answer:
**Reimer–Tiemann reaction** — phenol is treated with chloroform and aqueous NaOH, and a $\ce{-CHO}$ group is introduced at the *ortho* position (salicylaldehyde is formed):

$$\ce{C6H5OH + CHCl3 + 3NaOH ->[340 K] o-HOC6H4CHO + 3NaCl + 2H2O}$$

The alkali first generates dichlorocarbene $\ce{:CCl2}$ from chloroform; the phenoxide ion attacks it at the ortho position, and hydrolysis of the resulting intermediate gives salicylic acid's aldehyde. If both ortho positions are blocked, the aldehyde enters the para position.

questions.question: Write a short note on Hoffmann bromamide reaction.
questions.answer:
**Hoffmann bromamide (degradation) reaction:** an amide is treated with bromine in aqueous or alcoholic KOH and gives a **primary amine with one carbon atom less** than the amide:

$$\ce{RCONH2 + Br2 + 4NaOH -> RNH2 + Na2CO3 + 2NaBr + 2H2O}$$

For example, acetamide gives methylamine. The mechanism proceeds through N-bromoamide → isocyanate → carbamic acid, which decarboxylates. Because the amine formed is one carbon shorter and is not contaminated with secondary or tertiary amines, this is the best laboratory method for preparing pure primary amines.

questions.question: Write a short note on diazotisation.
questions.answer:
**Diazotisation** is the conversion of a primary aromatic amine into a benzene diazonium salt by treatment with nitrous acid (generated *in situ* from $\ce{NaNO2}$ and HCl) at low temperature:

$$\ce{C6H5NH2 + NaNO2 + 2HCl ->[273-278 K] C6H5N2^+Cl^- + NaCl + 2H2O}$$

Aniline therefore gives benzene diazonium chloride, $\ce{PhN2^+Cl^-}$, a stable salt only in the cold — the temperature must be kept at 273–278 K, otherwise it decomposes to phenol and nitrogen. Diazonium salts are extremely useful intermediates: they can be converted to phenols, halides, cyanides, and coupled with phenols or amines to give azo dyes.

questions.question: What happens when toluene is treated with conc. HNO$_3$ and H$_2$SO$_4$?
questions.answer:
Toluene undergoes **electrophilic aromatic nitration**. The $\ce{-CH3}$ group is ortho/para directing and activating, so a mixture of **2-nitrotoluene and 4-nitrotoluene** is obtained, with the para isomer as the major product:

$$\ce{C6H5CH3 + HNO3 ->[H2SO4, 30 ^\circ C] o- and p-CH3C6H4NO2 + H2O}$$

The nitrating species is the nitronium ion $\ce{NO2+}$. With excess acid and higher temperature further nitration gives 2,4-dinitro- and finally 2,4,6-trinitrotoluene (TNT).

questions.question: What happens when nitroethane is boiled with dilute HCl?
questions.answer:
Nitroethane is hydrolysed to **acetic acid** and **hydroxylammonium chloride** — the N–C bond of the nitro group is cleaved under acid hydrolysis:

$$\ce{C2H5NO2 + H2O + HCl -> CH3COOH + NH2OH.HCl}$$

The carbon chain is thereby shortened by one carbon because the carbon that carried the nitro group leaves as the carboxyl carbon of acetic acid.

questions.question: What is Bakelite? How is Buna-S obtained?
questions.answer:
**Bakelite** is the first thermosetting synthetic resin — a cross-linked phenol–formaldehyde (Novolac-type) polymer. Phenol condenses with formaldehyde, and on heating with a cross-linking agent (hexamethylenetetramine or more formaldehyde) a rigid three-dimensional network is built up. Because the chains are joined by strong covalent cross-links, Bakelite cannot be softened by reheating, is a good electrical insulator and is used for switch boards, plugs and handles.

**Buna-S** (styrene–butadiene rubber, SBR) is a *copolymer* obtained by the free-radical (peroxide-catalysed) emulsion polymerisation of **1,3-butadiene and styrene** in the ratio 3:1:

$$\ce{nCH2=CH-CH=CH2 + nC6H5CH=CH2 ->[-CH2-CH=CH-CH2-CH(C6H5)-CH2-]_n}$$

The product is a tough, abrasion-resistant rubber used chiefly for motor tyres; it is superior to natural rubber in resistance to wear and to oils.

questions.question: Determine the oxidation states of the central metal ion in: (a) K$_3$[Fe(CN)$_6$] (b) [PtCl$_4$]$^{2-}$ (c) [CoBr$_2$(CN)$_2$]$^{3-}$
questions.answer:
**(a) K$_3$[Fe(CN)$_6$]:** the complex ion is [Fe(CN)$_6$]$^{3-}$. Let $x$ be the oxidation state of Fe; CN$^-$ carries −1 each:

$$x + 6(-1) = -3 \Rightarrow x = +3$$

So **Fe is in the +3 state** (ferricyanide).

**(b) [PtCl$_4$]$^{2-}$:** with four chloride ligands,

$$x + 4(-1) = -2 \Rightarrow x = +2$$

So **Pt is +2** (tetrachloroplatinate(II)).

**(c) [CoBr$_2$(CN)$_2$]$^{3-}$:**

$$x + 2(-1) + 2(-1) = -3 \Rightarrow x - 4 = -3 \Rightarrow x = +1$$

So **Co is in the +1 state**.

In each case the counter-ion charges are added to the overall charge of the ion to make the sum zero, and the ligands (Cl$^-$, Br$^-$, CN$^-$) are treated as −1 each.

questions.question: What is the difference between soaps and detergents?
questions.answer:
| Soap | Detergent |
|---|---|
| Sodium or potassium salt of a long-chain fatty acid, made from vegetable oils/fats (e.g. sodium stearate, C$_{17}$H$_{35}$COO$^-$Na$^+$) | Sodium salt of a long-chain alkylbenzene sulphonic acid, made from petroleum products |
| The ionic head is a carboxylate, —COO$^-$ | The ionic head is a sulphonate, —SO$_3^-$ |
| Works only in **soft water**; with hard water the Ca$^{2+}$/Mg$^{2+}$ ions give insoluble calcium and magnesium soaps (scum) | Works in **both soft and hard water**, because the calcium and magnesium sulphonates are soluble |
| Biodegradable, but its manufacture consumes edible oils | Some branched-chain types are non-biodegradable and cause foaming in rivers; modern linear types are biodegradable |
| Less effective in acidic water (the acid is insoluble) | Effective over a wide pH range |

Both act by the same principle: the long hydrocarbon tail dissolves the grease while the ionic head keeps the micelle in water.

questions.question: Name the following: (a) Water soluble vitamin (b) A fat soluble vitamin (c) The disease caused by deficiency of vitamin C.
questions.answer:
(a) **Water-soluble vitamins:** B-group vitamins (B$_1$, B$_2$, B$_3$, B$_5$, B$_6$, B$_7$, B$_9$, B$_{12}$) and **vitamin C** (ascorbic acid). They must be supplied daily because the excess is excreted in urine.

(b) **Fat-soluble vitamins:** **A, D, E and K.** They are stored in the liver and adipose tissue, so a deficiency takes longer to develop but an excess can be toxic.

(c) **Deficiency of vitamin C causes scurvy** — bleeding gums, loosening of teeth, slow wound healing and anaemia, because vitamin C is needed for the synthesis of collagen.

questions.question: What happens when methyl chloride is treated with alcoholic KCN?
questions.answer:
Methyl chloride undergoes **nucleophilic substitution** — the cyanide ion is a good nucleophile and displaces Cl$^-$ (an S$_N$2 reaction, favoured here because the substrate is primary):

$$\ce{CH3Cl + KCN(alc) -> CH3CN + KCl}$$

The product is **methyl cyanide (acetonitrile), CH$_3$CN** — a nitrile. This is important synthetically because hydrolysis of the nitrile gives acetic acid, so the reaction lengthens the carbon chain by one carbon.

questions.question: What happens when ethyl chloride is treated with alcoholic KOH?
questions.answer:
Alcoholic KOH brings about **dehydrohalogenation** — an elimination of HCl rather than substitution:

$$\ce{CH3CH2Cl + KOH(alc) -> CH2=CH2 + KCl + H2O}$$

The product is **ethylene (ethene)**. The alcoholic solvent favours elimination (the OH$^-$ acts as a base, removing a $\beta$-hydrogen) whereas aqueous KOH would favour substitution to ethanol — a good illustration of how the solvent controls the outcome.

questions.question: What happens when chloroform is heated with Ag powder?
questions.answer:
Chloroform is **dehalogenated** by silver powder to give **acetylene (ethyne)**:

$$\ce{2CHCl3 + 6Ag -> C2H2 + 6AgCl}$$

Silver removes the chlorine as AgCl, and two CH units join to form the triple bond. (The printed key writes it with a single CHCl$_3$ molecule; the balanced equation needs two.)

questions.question: Can we use a copper vessel to store 1 M AgNO$_3$ solution? Given $E^\circ_{Ag^+/Ag}=0.80$ V, $E^\circ_{Cu^{2+}/Cu}=+0.34$ V. Explain.
questions.answer:
**No.** The cell made of Cu | Cu$^{2+}$ || Ag$^+$ | Ag has

$$E^\circ_{cell}=E^\circ_{cathode}-E^\circ_{anode}=E^\circ_{Ag^+/Ag}-E^\circ_{Cu^{2+}/Cu}=0.80-0.34=+0.46\ \text{V}$$

Since $E^\circ_{cell}$ is positive, the reaction

$$\ce{Cu(s) + 2Ag^+(aq) -> Cu^{2+}(aq) + 2Ag(s)}$$

is spontaneous. The copper vessel would be oxidised and dissolve while silver plates out on it, so the AgNO$_3$ solution would be contaminated and the vessel corroded. A glass or plastic container is therefore used, not a metal one. Copper can, however, safely hold solutions of less noble metal ions such as Zn$^{2+}$.

questions.question: For a reaction the energy of activation is zero. What is the value of rate constant at 300 K, if $k=1.6\times10^{6}$ s$^{-1}$ at 280 K? ($R=8.31$ J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$)
questions.answer:
Use the two-temperature form of the Arrhenius equation:

$$\log\frac{k_2}{k_1}=\frac{E_a}{2.303R}\left(\frac{1}{T_1}-\frac{1}{T_2}\right)$$

Here $E_a=0$, $T_1=280$ K, $T_2=300$ K, $k_1=1.6\times10^{6}$ s$^{-1}$.

$$\log\frac{k_2}{1.6\times10^{6}}=\frac{0}{2.303\times8.31}\left(\frac{1}{280}-\frac{1}{300}\right)=0=\log 1$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{k_2}{1.6\times10^{6}}=1\ \Rightarrow\ k_2=1.6\times10^{6}\ \text{s}^{-1}$$

The rate constant is **unchanged at $1.6\times10^{6}$ s$^{-1}$**. This is physically sensible: with zero activation energy the rate is limited only by the frequency of collisions and the Arrhenius factor $e^{-E_a/RT}=1$ is independent of temperature.

questions.question: Name the principal ore of aluminium.
questions.answer:
**Bauxite**, Al$_2$O$_3$·2H$_2$O (hydrated aluminium oxide). It is the principal ore, formed by the weathering of aluminium-bearing rocks.

*(Related minerals: cryolite Na$_3$AlF$_6$, used as a flux to lower the melting point in the electrolytic cell; corundum Al$_2$O$_3$, which is the anhydrous oxide; and kaolinite, a clay.)*

questions.question: Describe the leaching of aluminium ore.
questions.answer:
**Leaching of bauxite (Baeyer's process).** The powdered ore is digested with concentrated aqueous NaOH at about 150–200 °C and 5–10 atm. Amphoteric alumina dissolves to give sodium meta-aluminate while the acidic and basic impurities — Fe$_2$O$_3$, TiO$_2$ and silica — remain insoluble and are filtered off as 'red mud':

$$\ce{Al2O3 + 2NaOH(aq) -> 2NaAlO2 + H2O}$$

The filtrate is diluted and seeded (or CO$_2$ is passed in), when pure aluminium hydroxide precipitates:

$$\ce{NaAlO2 + 2H2O -> NaOH + Al(OH)3 v}$$

On strong heating the hydroxide gives pure alumina:

$$\ce{2Al(OH)3 ->[\Delta] Al2O3 + 3H2O}$$

This pure Al$_2$O$_3$ is then dissolved in molten cryolite and electrolysed (Hall–Héroult process) to give aluminium metal. Leaching thus concentrates the ore from a mixture of oxides to nearly pure alumina.

questions.question: Balance: (a) XeF$_2$ + H$_2$O = (b) MnO$_2$ + HCl = (c) I$_2$ + NaIO$_3$ = (with base)
questions.answer:
**(a)** Xenon difluoride hydrolyses, being both oxidised and reduced (disproportionation):

$$\ce{2XeF2 + 2H2O -> 2Xe + 4HF + O2}$$

**(b)** Manganese dioxide with concentrated HCl — the laboratory preparation of chlorine:

$$\ce{MnO2 + 4HCl -> MnCl2 + Cl2 + 2H2O}$$

**(c)** Iodine with sodium iodate in alkaline medium — iodic acid and hydriodic acid comproportionate to iodide/iodate only, but with I$_2$ and NaIO$_3$ in base the balanced equation is

$$\ce{I2 + 2NaIO3 -> 2NaIO3 + I2}$$

is not a reaction; the correct comproportionation to iodate is

$$\ce{3I2 + 6NaOH -> 5NaI + NaIO3 + 3H2O}$$

where iodine disproportionates to iodide and iodate. (The paper's printed equation, $\ce{I2 + 2NaClO3 -> 2NaIO3 + Cl2}$, is the oxidation of iodine by sodium chlorate.)

questions.question: Define colligative properties of dilute solution. The vapour pressure of a 2% aqueous solution of a non-volatile solute X at 373 K is 755 torr. Calculate the molar mass of the solute. (Vapour pressure of water at 373 K is 760 torr.)
questions.answer:
**Colligative properties** are those properties of a dilute solution which depend only on the *number* of solute particles and not on their nature — relative lowering of vapour pressure, elevation of boiling point, depression of freezing point and osmotic pressure.

**Calculation.** For a dilute solution Raoult's law gives the relative lowering of vapour pressure as the mole fraction of the solute:

$$\frac{p^\circ-p_s}{p^\circ}=\frac{n_B}{n_A+n_B}\approx\frac{n_B}{n_A}=\frac{W_B/M_B}{W_A/M_A}$$

Here $p^\circ=760$ torr, $p_s=755$ torr, $W_A=98$ g of water ($M_A=18$ g mol$^{-1}$), $W_B=2$ g, and $M_B$ is to be found:

$$\frac{760-755}{760}=\frac{2/M_B}{98/18}\ \Rightarrow\ \frac{5}{760}=0.00658=\frac{2/M_B}{5.444}$$

$$\frac{2}{M_B}=0.00658\times5.444=0.0358\ \Rightarrow\ M_B=\frac{2}{0.0358}\approx56\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$$

**The molar mass of X is about 56 g mol$^{-1}$** — a reasonable value for a small molecule (urea, for instance, is 60). The printed key's 55.47 g mol$^{-1}$ comes from the same arithmetic rounded differently.

*Note:* the paper prints the vapour pressure as "75 torr" in one place, which would make the numbers physically impossible for a 2% solution; its own worked answer uses the 5 torr lowering, i.e. 755 torr.

questions.question: What is ammonolysis of ester?
questions.answer:
**Ammonolysis** is the reaction of an ester with ammonia (or an amine), in which the alkoxy group is replaced by an amino group and an **amide** is formed:

$$\ce{CH3COOC2H5 + NH3 -> CH3CONH2 + C2H5OH}$$

Ethyl acetate therefore gives acetamide and ethanol. With excess amine, primary amines can be carried further to secondary and tertiary amides. It is the nitrogen analogue of hydrolysis and is used to prepare amides without going through the acid chloride.

questions.question: How will you convert acetaldehyde to acetamide and methanol to acetic acid?
questions.answer:
**Acetaldehyde → acetamide** (two routes):

Oxidation to acetic acid, conversion to the acid chloride, then ammonolysis:

$$\ce{CH3CHO ->[O][alk.KMnO4] CH3COOH ->[PCl5] CH3COCl ->[NH3] CH3CONH2}$$

or, more directly, oxidation to the acid followed by heating its ammonium salt:

$$\ce{CH3COOH ->[NH3] CH3COONH4 ->[\Delta] CH3CONH2 + H2O}$$

**Methanol → acetic acid:**

Methanol is first converted to methyl chloride, then to methyl cyanide, which is hydrolysed:

$$\ce{CH3OH ->[PCl5] CH3Cl ->[KCN] CH3CN ->[H3O^+] CH3COOH}$$

(Catalytic carbonylation, $\ce{CH3OH + CO ->[Rh/I^-] CH3COOH}$, is the industrial route.)

questions.question: What is Lanthanoid Contraction? Give two examples of Lanthanoid elements. What are the oxidation states exhibited by Lanthanoid elements?
questions.answer:
**Lanthanoid contraction** is the steady *decrease in the atomic and ionic radii* of the lanthanoids (the tripositive $\ce{Ln^{3+}}$ ions in particular) with increasing atomic number across the series.

The cause is **poor shielding of the 4f electrons**. As the atomic number increases by one, an extra electron enters the deep-lying 4f subshell, which screens the outer electrons from the nucleus only very weakly. The effective nuclear charge therefore rises steadily, pulling the outer shells in — the total contraction from La to Lu is only about 15 pm, but it is cumulative and has important consequences (e.g. Zr and Hf are almost identical in size and occur together in nature, and the lanthanoids are difficult to separate).

**Examples:** **Lanthanum (La, Z = 57)** and **Cerium (Ce, Z = 58)** — or any other member of the series such as neodymium or gadolinium.

**Oxidation states:** the characteristic and most stable state is **+3** (all lanthanoids form $\ce{Ln^{3+}}$). **+2** is shown by Eu, Yb and Sm, and **+4** by Ce, Tb, Pr and Nd — giving the series the oxidation states **+2, +3 and +4**.
